newsitem.title: USA: France and U.S. in war of words over Africa.
newsitem.headline: France and U.S. in war of words over Africa.

text.p: Warren Christopher has travelled more than 700,000 miles (1.1 million km) as U.S. secretary of state but never has a trip prompted the kind of reaction France leveled at his five-nation African tour, which ended on Monday.
Paris fired the opening salvo, suggesting U.S. efforts to organise an all-African military force to deal with crises on the continent trespassed onto traditional French territory.

"Since (President) Bill Clinton hasn't been to Africa once, since he didn't even mention Africa in his speech before the U.N. General Assembly, and since U.S. foreign development aid has diminished by 15 percent, I am delighted to see the president showing interest in Africa and making it a priority three weeks before the presidential elections," Jacques Godfrain, France's minister for foreign cooperation, said.

Critical exchanges between the two Nato allies have happened before and will again. Paris and Washington remain close allies despite differences over issues like Iraq. But Godfrain's words were unusually withering, and Christopher's response went far beyond his normally genteel and diplomatic demeanor.

"All nations must cooperate, not compete, if we are going to make a positive difference in Africa's future," Christopher said pointedly in a speech in South Africa. "The time has passed when Africa could be carved into spheres of influence, or when outside powers could view whole groups of states as their private domain. Today, Africa needs the support of all its many friends, not the exclusive patronage of a few."

Christopher did not mention France by name in his speech on Saturday, but the reference was clear. "The French are upset because they consider Africa to be their private domain. They feel threatened if others also want to make a contribution," one senior U.S. official said later.
Christopher apparently stung Paris by launching his first tour of the sub-Sahara and Mali in West Africa, where France once was the colonial power and still has influence.

France's legacy in Africa is mixed. So is the U.S. record. The closest the United States got to an African colony was Liberia, founded by freed American slaves. Now Washington has refused to intervene in the civil war there. It might have been different during the Cold War when Soviet moves in Africa often triggered a U.S. response.

Christopher tried to demonstrate a more intense U.S. engagement in Africa by pressing leaders to join a U.S.-organised all-African force to be deployed in time of crisis for humanitarian purposes under the United Nations.
He also exhorted them to propose alternate candidates for U.N. secretary-general to replace Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, whose reappointment Washington has vowed to veto.
All this proved too much for France, which U.S. officials say is having a hard time coping with its declining prestige. U.S. officials blame French President Jacques Chirac for the trouble-making.

They say he is trying to "recreate the French empire" and assert himself as "DeGaulle II," a reference to the late President Charles DeGaulle, who asserted French pre-eminence in the world and challenged American leadership by withdrawing France from the Western alliance's military structure.
Initially, after taking office in May 1995, Chirac seemed to be cooperating with Washington. But frictions between the United States and France seem to be mounting.

France has threatened to use its veto in the choice of a new secretary-general if the United States makes good on its pledge to veto Boutros-Ghali's reappointment. Paris also said it may not achieve full military integration in Nato in 1997 as planned if a Frenchman is not named to head the alliance's Southern Command in Italy.

U.S officials believe France's primary motive for the war of words over Africa is political. Some say France also worries about the United States becoming too much of an economic challenger on the continent.
